title: Gravitational waves
what: GW150914, the first gravitational wave ever heard, on 14 September 2015, told as a story in four chapters: its source, two black holes merging 1.3 billion light-years away; its journey to Earth; what it does to space as it passes, a ring of free masses stretched and squeezed; and how LIGO Livingston heard it, with what both detectors measured.
how: A gravitational wave stretches space across its path one way while squeezing it the other, then the other way round, and moves nothing along its path. To first order, a wave coming along z moves a free mass at (x, y) by ½(h₊x + h×y) across and ½(h×x − h₊y) up, where h₊ and h× are its two polarisations (the plus and the cross), taken at the moment the wave reaches it; areas are kept. The ring and its grid are moved by exactly that. The wave is GW150914 as LIGO measured it, from the data GWOSC publishes for the discovery paper’s Figure 1: the numerical-relativity waveform that best fits what Livingston recorded, from about 0.17 s before the merger, near 35 Hz, to the ringing of the black hole the two made, near 250 Hz, its strain rising to about 1.0 × 10⁻²¹. It is drawn face on, where both polarisations are equally strong and a quarter cycle apart: h₊ is the waveform at Livingston and h× the same a quarter cycle on. GW150914 was seen nearly face on or face off, so this is close to the wave that came; a detector records a mix of the two. Its card gives the event’s facts as the paper gives them, with their ranges. Behind the ring, sheets of points show the space the wave has crossed, each met by it a little earlier: the wave is drawn far slower than light, so that its wavelength (about 3,000 km at 100 Hz) fits the picture. At Livingston, the detector is drawn from above, north at the top, its two arms on their true bearings (LALSuite’s detector constants) and a unit long for their 4 km. The wave stretches one arm by half the strain Livingston measured and shrinks the other by as much, at the same 4 × 10²⁰; the light at the output is drawn brightening with the difference, from dark when they are equal (in LIGO it is held near dark, and the change is a tiny share of a fringe). Beneath, the strain both detectors measured, as Figure 1 draws it: Hanford’s shifted 6.9 ms earlier and turned upside down, as its arms lie the other way about, so it lies on Livingston’s; the best fit faint behind; a cursor and a clock follow the wave. “Hear it” plays the wave as a tone following its pitch and loudness, slowed 10 times and raised two octaves to be heard; it plays only when asked. The source is drawn from above its orbit: the two black holes at their masses’ ratio, going round at half the wave’s frequency (the orbit’s phase is half the wave’s, read from the waveform), closing in as the pitch rises by Kepler’s third law, then one. The sheet is the plane of their orbit. Each point of it is raised by the wave there: the h₊ the wave had as it left the source r/c earlier, turned by twice the point’s azimuth, at half strength (in the orbit’s plane only h₊ remains, halved) and weaker as 1/r. The two-armed spiral comes out of that, not drawn: its wavelength halves as the pitch doubles. The journey crosses 1.3 billion years in seconds, its years counted down, then plays the wave’s loudest tenth of a second at Earth, 100 times slower, its clock in UTC to the millisecond. So far from its source the wave is a plane wave: flat wavefronts across its path, a wavelength apart (c/f: about 8,600 km at 35 Hz, 3,000 km at 100 Hz, 1,200 km at 250 Hz), so several crests cross Earth at once. Each point of the space about Earth, drawn as a lattice, and each point of Earth is moved by the wave as it is where that point lies along the path, by the same first-order formula as the ring, at the same 4 × 10²⁰: Earth is seen squashed and stretched across the wave’s path. The merger’s wave reaches Livingston when the measured waveform peaks there, and Hanford 6.9 ms later, the measured delay. The story plays its chapters in turn, each from its own link (chapter=source, journey, space or detector); with less motion asked for, each holds still at its moment and waits to be stepped.
certainty: Stretched 4 × 10²⁰ times and slowed 100 times, to be seen: over LIGO’s 4 km arms the real change was about 4 × 10⁻¹⁸ m, a four-hundredth of a proton’s width.

The ring plays the best-fit waveform, not the measured strain itself, which is noisy: at Livingston and Hanford what was measured follows it within the noise, as Figure 1 shows. Hanford saw it 6.9 ms later and upside down, as its arms lie to Livingston’s.

Near the black holes, the source chapter’s formula does not hold: space is strongly curved there and the wave is not yet formed (it is worked out for a place many wavelengths away). The sheet fades out there, and the black holes’ sizes and distance apart are drawn as their masses’ ratio, not to the sheet’s scale. The wave is drawn far slower than light, so its wavelength fits the sheet.

Earth is drawn deformed as free space is, 4 × 10²⁰ times over: in truth its width changed by about 10⁻¹⁴ m (10⁻²¹ of 12,700 km), some eight protons across, and Earth, being solid and held together by its own forces, gave even less than free space does. It is drawn so to show what the wave does, not what any instrument could see.
others: Where in the sky it came from is the least certain part. Two detectors fix only the angle between the wave’s path and the line between them, so the paper places the source in a band of about 600 square degrees, mostly in the southern sky (90% credible), not at a point. The journey draws one way that fits: of all the directions that give the 6.9 ms, the most southern.
